question: To help prevent a set of doubles or triples from rolling over, a driver should do what when approaching corners, ramps, and curves?
choice_a: Steer gently and go slowly
choice_b: Speed up slightly to maintain momentum through the turn
choice_c: Brake hard just before entering the curve
choice_d: Shift into neutral to let the trailers align themselves
explanation: The manual states that to prevent trailers from rolling over, you must steer gently and go slowly around corners, on ramps, off ramps, and curves.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.1 Prevent Trailer from Rolling Over

question: In a set of doubles or triples, which trailer is most likely to turn over as a result of the crack-the-whip effect?
choice_a: The first trailer directly behind the tractor
choice_b: The last trailer in the combination
choice_c: The converter dolly itself
choice_d: All trailers turn over at exactly the same rate
explanation: The manual states that doubles and triples are more likely to turn over because of the crack-the-whip effect, and the last trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.2 Beware of the Crack-the-whip Effect

question: Why must a driver of doubles or triples look far ahead down the road?
choice_a: So lane changes and speed reductions can be made gradually to avoid rollover or jackknife
choice_b: So the driver can read road signs before other traffic does
choice_c: It is only necessary at night
choice_d: It reduces the need to inspect the coupling before a trip
explanation: Doubles and triples must be driven very smoothly to avoid rollover or jackknife, so the driver should look far ahead to slow down or change lanes gradually when necessary.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.4 Look Far Ahead

question: Because doubles and triples are longer and cannot be turned or stopped as suddenly as other vehicles, a driver should do what?
choice_a: Allow more following distance and make sure of large enough gaps before entering or crossing traffic
choice_b: Follow more closely to keep the combination compact
choice_c: Avoid using turn signals since the extra length makes them unnecessary
choice_d: Only change lanes at night when traffic is light
explanation: The manual explains that because doubles and triples are longer and need more space, drivers should allow more following distance and be certain of large enough gaps before entering or crossing traffic.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1 Pulling Double/Triple Trailers

question: Why must a driver be especially careful driving double and triple bottoms in bad weather or mountain driving?
choice_a: There is greater length and more dead axles to pull, creating more chance for skids and loss of traction
choice_b: The extra trailers make the brakes stronger than needed
choice_c: Doubles and triples are not allowed on mountain roads
choice_d: Dead axles improve traction in bad weather
explanation: The manual states that in adverse conditions you have greater length and more dead axles to pull with your drive axles than other drivers, meaning more chance for skids and loss of traction.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.6 Adverse Conditions

question: When parking a set of doubles or triples, a driver should be especially aware of what?
choice_a: How parking lots are arranged, to avoid getting into a spot that cannot be pulled straight through
choice_b: Whether the parking lot has painted lines
choice_c: The exact number of other trucks already parked
choice_d: Whether the converter dolly needs to be washed
explanation: The manual warns drivers to be aware of how parking lots are arranged to avoid a long and difficult escape, and to not get into a spot they cannot pull straight through.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.7 Parking the Vehicle

question: Converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: January 1, 2000
choice_c: July 1, 2017
choice_d: September 9, 2022
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have antilock brakes and will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.8 Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: How can a driver tell that a converter dolly is equipped with antilock brakes?
choice_a: It will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly
choice_b: It will have a red lamp on the pintle hook
choice_c: It will have a green sticker on the tow bar
choice_d: There is no external way to tell
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies with the required antilock brakes will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.1.8 Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: If the second (rear) trailer does not have spring brakes, how does a driver set its emergency brakes before coupling?
choice_a: Drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, then disconnect the emergency line
choice_b: Simply apply the trailer's parking brake lever by hand
choice_c: Disconnect the light cord and wait ten minutes
choice_d: Fill the fuel tank and let the engine idle for one hour
explanation: The manual explains that if the second trailer lacks spring brakes, connecting the emergency line, charging the trailer air tank, and then disconnecting the emergency line sets the trailer emergency brakes if the slack adjusters are correctly adjusted.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: What should a driver do if there is any doubt about whether the second trailer's brakes are set before coupling?
choice_a: Chock the wheels
choice_b: Disconnect the fifth wheel
choice_c: Skip the coupling procedure entirely
choice_d: Remove the spare tire
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to chock the wheels if there is any doubt about whether the second trailer's brakes are properly set.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: For the safest handling on the road in a set of doubles, where should the more heavily loaded semitrailer be positioned?
choice_a: In the first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear
choice_b: In the rear position, with the lighter trailer directly behind the tractor
choice_c: It does not matter which trailer is loaded heavier
choice_d: Split evenly between the converter dolly and the tractor frame
explanation: The manual states that for the safest handling, the more heavily loaded semitrailer should be in the first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: What is a converter dolly?
choice_a: A coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel that allows a semitrailer to be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination
choice_b: A hand tool used to tighten the pintle hook
choice_c: A brake valve mounted only on the third trailer
choice_d: A type of tire chock used only on tank vehicles
explanation: The manual defines a converter dolly (converter gear) as a coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semitrailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: Before backing the converter dolly under the rear trailer, what must be true about the trailer's height?
choice_a: The trailer must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel so it is raised slightly as the dolly is pushed under
choice_b: The trailer must be exactly level with the ground
choice_c: The trailer must be higher than the tractor's fifth wheel
choice_d: Trailer height does not matter for coupling the dolly
explanation: The manual states that trailer height must be correct -- slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel -- so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under it.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: When making a visual check of the coupling between the converter dolly and the rear trailer, what should a driver look for?
choice_a: No visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, with locking jaws closed on the kingpin
choice_b: A gap of about one inch between the fifth wheel plates
choice_c: The safety chains hanging loose
choice_d: The landing gear fully lowered
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to make a visual check of the coupling to confirm there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel and that the locking jaws are closed on the kingpin.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: When uncoupling the rear trailer, why does a driver lower the landing gear of the second semitrailer before disconnecting?
choice_a: To remove some weight from the converter dolly
choice_b: To disconnect the light cords automatically
choice_c: To raise the tank pressure
choice_d: It is done only for cosmetic inspection purposes
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to lower the landing gear of the second semitrailer enough to remove some weight from the dolly during the uncoupling procedure.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers

question: Why should a driver never unlock the pintle hook while the converter dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choice_a: The dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it difficult to re-couple
choice_b: It will drain all the air from the trailer emergency line instantly
choice_c: It voids the manufacturer's warranty on the fifth wheel
choice_d: It automatically triggers the antilock brake system
explanation: The manual warns that unlocking the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer can cause the dolly tow bar to fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers

question: When coupling a triple-trailer rig, what is the correct order of operations after the tractor is coupled to the first trailer?
choice_a: Move the converter dolly into position and couple the first trailer to the second trailer using the method for coupling doubles
choice_b: Couple the third trailer to the tractor first, then work backward
choice_c: Couple all three trailers to the tractor simultaneously
choice_d: Attach the third trailer directly to the first trailer without a dolly
explanation: The manual describes coupling the tractor to the first trailer, then moving the converter dolly into position and coupling the first trailer to the second trailer using the same method used for coupling doubles.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.3 Coupling and Uncoupling Triple Trailers

question: When uncoupling a triple-trailer rig, which trailer is uncoupled first?
choice_a: The third trailer, by pulling the dolly out and then unhitching it using the doubles method
choice_b: The first trailer directly behind the tractor
choice_c: Whichever trailer is heaviest
choice_d: All three trailers are released at the same time
explanation: The manual states that to uncouple a triple-trailer rig, the third trailer is uncoupled first by pulling the dolly out and then unhitching the dolly using the method for uncoupling doubles.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.2.3 Coupling and Uncoupling Triple Trailers

question: When inspecting the lower fifth wheel on a combination vehicle, the locking jaws should be closed around what part of the kingpin?
choice_a: The shank, not the head, of the kingpin
choice_b: The head, not the shank, of the kingpin
choice_c: The kingpin's release arm only
choice_d: The grease fitting on top of the kingpin
explanation: The manual specifies that when checking the lower fifth wheel, the locking jaws should be around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

question: Why should a driver check that the fifth wheel is not positioned too far forward on the frame?
choice_a: So the tractor frame does not hit the landing gear, or the cab does not hit the trailer, during turns
choice_b: So the converter dolly can be attached more easily
choice_c: So the antilock brake lamp remains visible
choice_d: Fifth wheel position has no effect on turning clearance
explanation: The manual warns to check that the fifth wheel is not so far forward that the tractor frame will hit the landing gear, or the cab will hit the trailer, during turns.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

question: On a set of doubles or triples, what should the shut-off valve position be at the rear of the front trailer(s) versus the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Rear of front trailers: OPEN. Rear of last trailer: CLOSED
choice_b: Rear of front trailers: CLOSED. Rear of last trailer: OPEN
choice_c: All shut-off valves should be OPEN at all times
choice_d: All shut-off valves should be CLOSED at all times
explanation: The manual specifies that the shut-off valves at the rear of front trailers should be OPEN, while the shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer should be CLOSED.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

topic: Converter Dolly Air Tank Drain Valve
question: During inspection of a set of doubles or triples, what position should the converter dolly's air tank drain valve be in?
choice_a: CLOSED
choice_b: OPEN
choice_c: Half open
choice_d: It has no drain valve
explanation: The manual states that the converter dolly air tank drain valve should be CLOSED during inspection.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

topic: Checking Air Flow to All Trailers
question: When checking that air flows to all trailers on a double or triple, what indicates the entire system is charged after opening the emergency line shut-off at the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Hearing air escaping at the rear
choice_b: Seeing the trailer air supply knob turn green
choice_c: The trailer brakes releasing immediately
choice_d: The engine RPM dropping
explanation: The manual states that after opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer, hearing air escaping shows the entire system is charged.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

question: When testing the tractor protection valve, at what approximate air pressure range should the trailer air supply control pop out to the emergency position?
choice_a: Usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi
choice_b: Usually within the range of 60 to 80 psi
choice_c: Exactly at 100 psi
choice_d: Exactly at 10 psi
explanation: The manual states that the trailer air supply control should pop out when air pressure falls into the range specified by the manufacturer, usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

question: What could happen if the tractor protection valve does not work properly?
choice_a: An air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control
choice_b: The converter dolly would automatically detach
choice_c: The trailer lights would stay on permanently
choice_d: Nothing significant would happen since the service brakes take over
explanation: The manual warns that if the tractor protection valve doesn't work properly, an air hose or trailer brake leak could drain all the air from the tractor, causing the emergency brakes to come on with possible loss of control.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

question: How does a driver test the trailer emergency brakes on a set of doubles or triples?
choice_a: Charge the trailer air brake system, check that the trailer rolls freely, then pull out the trailer air supply control and pull gently on the trailer to check that the emergency brakes are on
choice_b: Simply look at the trailer air supply knob without moving the vehicle
choice_c: Disconnect the light cords and observe if the trailer moves
choice_d: Rev the engine to maximum RPM while parked
explanation: The manual describes charging the trailer air brake system, checking that the trailer rolls freely, then stopping and pulling out the trailer air supply control (or placing it in the emergency position) and pulling gently on the trailer to confirm the emergency brakes are on.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

question: How should a driver test the trailer service brakes during the air brake check, and how are trailer brakes normally controlled during regular operation?
choice_a: Test with the hand control (trolley valve) to feel the brakes come on, but control them normally with the foot pedal
choice_b: Test only with the foot pedal, and never use the hand control for any purpose
choice_c: Test by disconnecting the emergency line and listening for a hiss
choice_d: Trailer service brakes cannot be tested separately from the tractor brakes
explanation: The manual explains that trailer brakes should be tested with the hand valve (trolley valve) but are controlled in normal operation with the foot pedal, which applies air to the service brakes at all wheels.
source_note: Indiana Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, cover-dated September 9, 2022), Indiana BMV/AAMVA -- Section 7, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks
